q.intro.text: A round plaza has a gate in its wall, from A to B. Three friends stand on the far side of the wall, at P, Q and R, and each measures how wide the gate looks: the angle between the lines to A and to B. Who sees the widest gate? Pick one, and say how sure you are.

q.cb.near.text: You said the friend nearest the gate sees it widest. Close up it does look bigger, but the angle is the same everywhere on that arc: half of arc A B. All three see exactly the same angle.

q.cb.same.text: You said all three see the same angle. The proof backs you: every one of them is an inscribed angle on arc A B, so each is half of that arc.

q.cb.across.text: You said the friend straight across sees it widest. Standing straight across feels central, but every point of that arc sees the gate at half of arc A B: the same angle.

e.intro.text: One circle, one arc, and three angles that stand on it.

e.step0.text: The central angle A O B has its vertex at the center. An arc's measure is its central angle: arc A B is one hundred degrees.

e.step1.text: Now the vertex C sits on the circle: an inscribed angle. Slide C along the arc: it reads fifty degrees the whole way. Half of the arc.

e.step2.text: Push C across the chord, onto arc A B itself. Now the angle opens onto the other arc, two hundred sixty degrees, and reads one hundred thirty degrees: still half its arc.

e.why.text: Why is the inscribed angle exactly half the central angle?

e.why.ok.text: Yes. Two radii make an isosceles triangle, and the central angle is its exterior angle: the sum of two equal angles. You prove it in a minute.

e.why.far.text: Distance is not it: C slid nearer and farther and the angle never changed.

e.why.look.text: Looking is not a reason. The readout says fifty, but a reason must say why for every position of C.

t.intro.text: Arc A B measures one hundred twenty-eight degrees. C, D and E are on the circle; E is on arc A B itself.

t.c.text: Worked: angle A C B is inscribed and stands on arc A B, so it is half: sixty-four degrees.

t.d.ask.text: Your turn: what is the measure of angle A D B?

t.d.ok.text: Right: D is on the same arc as C, so it sees the same arc A B. Same arc, same angle.

t.d.full.text: That is the whole arc. An angle with its vertex on the circle is half its arc.

t.d.supp.text: D is on the same side of the chord as C: same arc, so the same angle, not the supplement.

t.d.other.text: Which arc does angle A D B open onto? Then take half of it.

t.e.ask.text: And the measure of angle A E B? E is on arc A B itself.

t.e.ok.text: Right: E opens onto the other arc, two hundred thirty-two degrees, and half of that is one hundred sixteen. Check: sixty-four plus one hundred sixteen is one hundred eighty.

t.e.same.text: E is on the other side of chord A B: it cannot see arc A B, it sees the major arc.

t.e.full.text: That is the major arc itself. Take half of it.

t.e.other.text: Find the arc E opens onto: three hundred sixty minus arc A B. Then halve it.

t.done.text: Same arc, same angle; across the chord, supplementary. Now prove why the angle is half.

p.intro.text: The easiest case first: the center O lies on side C B, so C B is a diameter. Call x the measure of angle A C B. Build the proof, then give every line its reason.

p.proved.text: Proved: x is half of arc A B. The other two cases, with the center inside or outside the angle, add or subtract two of these.

p.plaza.text: Back to the plaza. The gate cuts off an arc of seventy degrees, and the three friends all stand on the other arc.

p.next.text: So how wide does the gate look to each friend?

p.next.ok.text: Right: each angle is inscribed on the same seventy degree arc, so each is thirty-five degrees.

p.next.near.text: Nearer does not mean wider: all three angles stand on the same arc.

p.next.full.text: Seventy is the arc. Their vertices are on the circle, so the angles are half of it.
